data.name: Jagvitha
data.gender_notes: Jagvitha is used as a unisex name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Jagat (universe) + Itha (residence or abode) = Jagvitha, Goddess of victory. She is the divine power that bestows victory and success upon her devotees. The name Jagvitha carries the meaning “Goddess of victory” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Jagvitha usually hope their child will grow to embody goddess of victory and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Represents strength, courage, and the power to overcome obstacles.
data.etymology: Jagvitha belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Goddess of victory.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Jagvitha total 6, giving a life-path number of 6. Number 6 is linked with Venus and with the qualities of responsibility, care and community.

data.cultural_impact: The name "Jagvitha" holds a significant place in the Hindu culture, symbolizing the victory of good over evil. This name is especially popular in certain regions, such as Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka, where the deity "Jagadeesh" or "Jagannatha" is revered. The name reminds us of the power of the divine, one that grants us success and victory when we call upon it.
data.spiritual_significance: On a deeper level, the name "Jagvitha" reflects the spiritual significance of the pursuit of victory in life. It is not merely about achieving success in the external world, but also about triumphing over inner struggles and vices. Devotion to Jagvitha can help us gain mastery over our thoughts, emotions, and actions, ultimately leading us towards spiritual growth and self-realization.
data.spiritual_symbolism: Jagvitha's name signifies the triumph of wisdom and inner light over darkness and ignorance. The syllables 'Jag' and 'Vitha' represent the dynamic interplay of consciousness and knowledge, suggesting continuous spiritual growth.

historical_references.reference: Jagatguru Jagadgamini Jagvitha Thirumalachar Swamigal, popularly known as Jagadguru Jagvithar, was a 16th-17th century Hindu philosopher and teacher who is considered to be one of the greatest exponents of Advaita Vedanta. He was born in Tamil Nadu, India, and was a direct disciple of Ramanuja. He wrote numerous commentaries and works on various texts, the most famous being the 'Vedantasara' and the 'Nalini Vijnana'. His teachings emphasized the non-dualistic philosophy of Advaita Vedanta and had a significant impact on the Hindu religious and philosophical traditions.

Jagadguru Jagvitha Sahasranshekara Swamigal, also known as Jagadguru Jagvithar, was a 19th century Hindu monk who was the 28th head of the Sringeri Sharada Peetham, a major Hindu institution for the study and propagation of Advaita Vedanta. He is known for his work on the 'Brahma Sutras' and his commentary on the 'Bhagavad Gita'. He was born in the village of Kudalasangam in the Tamil Nadu region of India. His teachings emphasized the importance of devotion to God and the non-dualistic philosophy of Advaita Vedanta. His influence extended beyond India to Sri Lanka, Nepal, and other parts of Asia.
